title: Mailbag: Harrison Smith’s Return; Vikings Roster Mechanics; 2026 Week 1 Arrives - Minnesota Vikings
content: Do you have a comment or question? Send it to the Mailbag. Every Monday we'll post several comments and/or questions. Click here to submit a comment or question to Mailbag. Remember to include your name and town in the email. If Twitter / X is your jam, you can send a question to me that way as well. The Hitman returneth — and just in time for the 2026 regular season. Harrison Smith and the Vikings on Saturday agreed to terms for the 2012 first-round pick to return to Minnesota for his 15th NFL season. Smith is back at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center this morning. The Vikings will open their 66th slate by hosting the Green Bay Packers at 3:25 p.m. (CT) Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium. Assuming he suits up, it will be the 27th Border Battle for Smith (out of 132 in the series). Memorably, the two teams met to conclude the 2025 season at the same venue, and Smith (just in case he didn't return) and C.J. Ham (who was playing in his final game) received tributes from the crowd. The Vikings also will be wearing their Classic uniforms for the second straight home game against the Packers. The rivalry rarely needs hype, but as an additional boost, CBS' THE NFL TODAY will be broadcasting on CBS from the Vikings Legacy Ship before the noon slate of games. Folks are encouraged to join the atmosphere, regardless of whether they have game tickets. The same goes for the free Vikings Kickoff Concert featuring Cole Swindell, which is scheduled to start at 1 p.m. in The Commons. View photos of the Vikings 53-man roster as of Sep. 5, 2026. I had a good idea Harrison Smith would return. But the silence was causing a slight vibration in my foundation. I was wondering if he wanted to skip camp and all the offseason rigor and save his health for "real" football. I know in the past some players have prolonged the decision to return for that reason. No matter now. He has experience on the field and the ability to influence and educate those around him. I figure Coach Flores is downright giddy like all of Viking Nation. Thank you, Hitman! We love you! Now start lighting people up! It was admittedly and unquestionably weird to produce the Vikings Yearbook and Playbook editions for Training Camp and the first preseason game without including Smith. He was in his third Vikings season when I started here, so it's become quite routine to see him patrolling the defense and doing un-routine things, adding to his candidacy for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Smith's knowledge of Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores' system, from the meeting room to his ability to bring it to life on the field should benefit young players who have joined an impressive core of veterans. Maybe he heard how much fun the crew had during those joint practices with Baltimore? We'll probably hear from Smith in a media session later this week, but I'd imagine he's kept up a strong training plan. The 53-man roster is now set, so the focus has to be on beating the Green Bay Packers on Sept. 13 at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis. How will Kyler Murray and the "Minnesota Moving Company" handle the Green Bay Packers defense? Everybody is talking about how good Kyler Murray, our WRs and TEs will be in 2026. That only happens if our OL plays well and stays healthy. I did not see much of anything this past preseason to make me confident, except for maybe a few plays against the Giants. If we can't run the ball on third-and-2, or Kyler is on his back or running for his life against the blitz, it all won't matter. It all comes down to our OL (again) so LETS GO!!! SKOL It's hard to say how any season will go, but the Vikings should be able to answer some internal and external questions right out of the gate. Murray is looking forward to making his first start for Minnesota after playing just nine offensive snaps in this year's preseason opener at the New York Giants. He and the Vikings first-team offense pivoted to Week 1 preparations when training camp finished. The starting offensive line hasn't appeared in a game together since popping an 18-yard run by Aaron Jones, Sr., on the inaugural snap of the preseason. The group was able to log substantial work in individual and team drills when Minnesota hosted Baltimore for joint practices. While there are sure to be plenty of eyeballs on Murray, I'm among those highly intrigued in seeing what the revamped run game looks like. I want to learn whether the offensive line is able to play on Green Bay's side of the line of scrimmage on run plays and provide a pocket that will keep Murray from needing to dip into his scrambling ability too often. Spoiler alert, we'll have a feature on Vikings.com this week about the revamped running game, so be on the lookout for that in addition to other content to get you prepared for the game. The group expected to play the most on Sunday has a very limited sample size in the public view this year, but I get the feeling the offensive line is eager to harvest the results of its hard work. I really like former Vikings running back Zavier Scott. He has a great story and he runs hard. I was surprised when he didn't make the team, but now I understand that they planned to add him to the practice squad if he cleared waivers. Unfortunately, the Bears are going to sign him. The team gambled and lost, but that's the way the system works. My question is this; do you think teams, especially division rivals, pick up players like that to pick their brains on what their previous teams offense and defense looks like? I suppose it's legal but, how does a team protect their secrets? — Mike Schuffenhauer, Fan from North Minneapolis since 1969 Scott is a player all Vikings fans can feel good about wishing well as he continues his career, except for any opportunities directly against the Vikings. He runs hard and works even harder, and he daily walks the walk of his faith. I'm sure Chicago's primary interest in signing him was to add a good, young player to its practice squad, but there could be a situation where the Bears try to learn more about Minnesota's new run game or protection calls or play designs from Scott, which could provide a little help in preparing for Week 2 when Chicago would only have one game film to review when researching this year's approach. View the best photos of Vikings safety Harrison Smith throughout his career as he announced he will return for his 15th season in 2026. Please describe the various amounts of money that practice squad players make? What kind of latitude do NFL teams have with deals for practice squad players? Might some be guaranteed deals? And how does the game check change when a player is elevated to the active roster? We heard from Vikings General Manager Nolan Teasley last week in his first comments since reducing the roster to the 53-man limit and establishing the practice squad, which is capped at 16 (or 17 with one International Player Pathway participant). One thing that was clear in Teasley's comments is his appreciation for the practice squad and his holistic view of the roster as 70 instead of 53. The practice squad continues to evolve and creates opportunities for players to be readily available. The sizes of practice squads have increased substantially since Teasley launched his career with Seattle in 2013. Players on practice squads can be poached at any point if another team signs the player to its 53. The Rochester Democrat and Chronicle just reported on practice squad salaries last week and noted players with two or fewer accrued seasons receive $13,750 per week, which would total $247,500 if a player was on the practice squad an entire season without being elevated. Practice squad players with more experience can negotiate for a range between $18,350 and 22,850 per week. According to the NFL Operations Manuel, if a player is elevated for a regular-season game, he receives the "applicable minimum salary for a player with his number of credited seasons (prorated for one week of regular-season pay or the applicable postseason amount). Practice squad players can be elevated three times in one League Year. After that, a subsequent elevation would require placement on the 53-man Active/Inactive list. "The team must then waive or terminate his player contract before the player can be re-signed to the practice squad. If the player is re-signed to the practice squad this way, the player is again eligible to be elevated for the previously mentioned maximum of three games." Ownership and the upper end of the team are really impressive, as are many of the position coaches, and both the offensive and defensive coordinators. It may not happen this year, but if they are able to keep this nucleus in place for two years, they are going to be very hard to beat as they win their first Super Bowl. We'll close today with a bit of positivity from Bruce. There have been intentional decisions backed by sound processes (player evaluations, analytics and reason) in trying to build the best possible team. Every squad will be challenged by something in the course of an NFL season, and some teams appear to have better fortunes than others with regard to injuries or bounces of the football. title: MPPSC Mains 2026 GS-1 Paper Analysis, Check Paper Level, Review & Questions Asked - PW
content: MPPSC Mains 2026 GS-1 Paper Analysis is detailed here. MPPSC Mains 2026 GS-1 was conducted on September 7, 2026. The paper balanced static MP History, Art & Culture, and Geography with manageable short and long descriptive questions. Check paper review here. The Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission (MPPSC) conducted the MPPSC Mains 2026 GS-1 Paper on September 7, 2026, marking the beginning of the State Service Main Examination schedule. Held in offline pen-and-paper mode across designated examination centers in Madhya Pradesh, General Studies Paper 1 evaluates candidate knowledge across History and Geography, with a dedicated emphasis on the state of Madhya Pradesh. Initial candidate feedback and expert evaluations indicate that the paper maintained a moderate difficulty level. While short-answer questions tested core static facts from Indian History and MP Culture, the long-answer analytical questions demanded well-structured, point-wise conceptual answers. The MPPSC Mains 2026 GS-1 Paper was moderate in difficulty. Compared with previous years, several questions were slightly more indirect, requiring candidates to understand the question carefully and apply their conceptual knowledge rather than relying solely on direct factual recall. Overall, candidates with strong conceptual clarity and good answer-writing practice were better positioned to handle the paper effectively. The examination structure followed the official Commission pattern for GS Paper 1, split evenly into Section A (History & Culture) and Section B (Geography). Exam Conducting Body: Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission (MPPSC) Exam Name: MPPSC State Service Main Examination 2026 Sections Covered: Section A – History & Culture | Section B – Geography Overall Difficulty Level: Moderate (Factual + Conceptual) The MPPSC GS-1 question paper was divided into two main sections. Candidates encountered direct static questions alongside state-specific applications. Section A tested Ancient, Medieval, and Modern Indian History, alongside World History and prominent historical movements of Madhya Pradesh. These include very short, short and long asnwer types questions. key topics included in the history section of the exam are- 1.1: Chanhudaro (Indus-Saraswati Civilization Site) 2.8: Contribution of Isuri in Bundeli Fag Tradition Section B balanced Physical Geography, Human & Economic Geography, Disaster Management, and Geographical Information Systems (GIS) with Madhya Pradesh Geography. These include very short, short and long asnwer types questions. key topics included in the geography section of the exam are- Nuclear Energy: Definition and major nuclear power stations/states in India National Bio-Energy Programme: Key features and leading states Major Earthquake Zones: Earthquake-prone zones in India Air Pollution: Key measures to control air pollution Rainfall in Madhya Pradesh: Causes of high rainfall in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the state Ken-Betwa Link Project: Key features, objectives, and significance The GS-1 paper carries a total weightage of 300 marks, structured into two equal sections of 150 marks each. Very Short Answer Questions (3 Marks / 2 Marks as per updated pattern): Require brief 1–2 sentence definitions or direct factual statements within specified word limits. Short Answer Questions (5 Marks / 7 Marks): Demand structured point-wise answers with sub-headings and key examples (approx. 50–60 words). Long Answer / Essay Type Questions (11 Marks / 10 Marks): Require comprehensive analytical answers including introduction, contextual body points, maps/diagrams, and a balanced conclusion (approx. 200 words). Master State-Specific Static Content: Over 40–50% of the paper explicitly targets Madhya Pradesh History, Culture, Geography, and Resource Distribution. Studying localized MP GK is crucial. Practice Map Drawing: In Geography long-answer questions, drawing quick outline maps of India and Madhya Pradesh boosts candidate scores significantly. Focus on Direct Answer Structuring: Given strict word and space limits in the MPPSC Mains answer booklet, direct point-wise presentation works better than lengthy introductory paragraphs. Dongsu Heo, Honorary Chairman of GS Caltex, Donates 100 Million Won to the Korea Golf Association Dongsu Heo, Honorary Chairman of GS Caltex, Kwangsoo Heo, Chairman of Samyang International, and Junhong Heo, Vice Chairman of SYTS, donated 100 million won for junior development to the Korea Golf Association. The donation was made on September 7, one day before the opening of the 72nd Heo Junggu Cup Korea Amateur Golf Championship. From the left, Junhong Heo, Vice Chairman of SYTS, Dongsu Heo, Honorary Chairman of GS Caltex, Hyungmo Kang, President of the Korea Golf Association, and Kwangsoo Heo, Chairman of Samyang International, are taking a commemorative photo at the junior development donation ceremony. Provided by Samyang International The Korea Amateur Golf Championship was established in 1954. Since 2003, the tournament has been held as the “Heo Junggu Cup” in honor of the late Junggu Heo, Honorary Chairman of SYTS and Samyang International, who was the first Korean member of the Royal & Ancient Golf Club (R&A), served as the 6th to 8th President of the Korea Golf Association, and was the founding President of the Korea Professional Golfers’ Association. This year, the event will be held over four days starting from September 8 at Namseoul Country Club in Seongnam, Gyeonggi Province. title: Hur Sae-hong charts GS Caltex’s path beyond refining - The Korea Herald
content:
Business Hur Sae-hong charts GS Caltex’s path beyond refining Published : Sept. 7, 2026 - 15:27:55
Updated : Sept. 7, 2026 - 18:01:39 Vice chair outlines GS Caltex’s lower-carbon transformation in McKinsey interview Amid sweeping changes in global energy markets, GS Caltex Vice Chair Hur Sae-hong seeks to move South Korea’s energy and chemical company beyond its decades-old focus on refining volumes toward higher-value, lower-carbon businesses. Hur outlined his vision in McKinsey & Co.’s “Leading Asia” interview series and its centennial book, “Shapers & Founders: The Untold Stories of Asia’s Extraordinary Owner-CEOs.” He was featured alongside other Korean business leaders from companies including HD Hyundai and MBK Partners. A fourth-generation member of GS Group’s founding family, Hur spent more than 18 years working in Japan, the US and Singapore for companies including IBM and Chevron. Those experiences helped shape a management philosophy that combines global adaptability with what he describes as traditional Korean humility. At its center is “we-dership,” Hur’s term for leadership built collectively. The idea calls on executives to “lead from the top, but move together,” with teamwork underpinning the company’s ambition to remain competitive for the next century. GS Caltex, Korea’s first private oil refiner, operates the world’s fourth-largest single-site refinery. The company prospered for decades on surging energy demand across Asia, but slowing global growth and the risk of excess supply have challenged its traditional volume-led model. “How can we maintain a growth path on a quality basis to ensure we remain sustainable for the future?” Hur said. His answer is what GS Caltex calls its “Deep Transformation Journey,” built around three pillars of transformation: business, digital and artificial intelligence, and green transformation. Business transformation, which the company calls BX, seeks to overhaul its mindset, culture and organizational structure. Digital and AI transformation, or DAX, focuses on building capabilities internally, including retraining and refining petrochemical engineers through an in-house digital academy. Green transformation, or GX, seeks to shift the company’s portfolio toward lower-carbon growth areas. These include sustainable aviation fuel, bio-based marine fuel, circular plastics, clean hydrogen, and carbon capture, utilization and storage. Hur is also pushing for GS Caltex to build what he calls a “black-box advantage” — an internal combination of work processes, organizational capabilities and corporate culture that competitors would struggle to replicate. Investing in emerging green businesses carries substantial risk, but Hur argues that standing still poses an even greater threat. He describes the status quo as “a killer of sustainable growth.” To manage that risk, GS Caltex uses marginal abatement cost curves to assess projects according to their cost and emissions-reduction potential, prioritizing lower-risk opportunities. Hur is also trying to preserve startuplike agility within a large corporation. A newly created "business council" brings senior executives together to lead cross-company strategic projects that might otherwise remain confined within individual business units. Named one of Stanford Graduate School of Business’ “Centennial Alumni Catalysts” in 2025, Hur said the success of the strategy would ultimately be judged by measurable results. “For me, sustainability means fundamentally rebalancing our portfolio toward lower-carbon businesses,” he said. “In the end, I believe the only way to demonstrate this commitment is through outcomes, not words.” S. title: JADES-GS-z14-0, a galaxy discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope, already contained oxygen less than 300 million years after the Big Bang — a finding confirmed by ALMA, suggesting generations of massive stars had already been born, lived and - Space Daily
content:
ALMA detected ionised oxygen in a galaxy seen before the universe was 300 million years old, supporting rapid stellar enrichment while leaving its exact history open. By Deep Field
·
Edited by
												Lachlan Brown JADES-GS-z14-0 already contained oxygen when the universe was less than 300 million years old. Two teams reported the detection using ALMA, the telescope array in Chile, in studies publicised in March 2025. Webb had discovered the galaxy and established its extreme distance; ALMA added a clear chemical signature and a much more precise redshift. The oxygen implies that stars had already made heavier elements and released them into surrounding gas. The suggestion of successive generations of massive stars is physically plausible, but the observation does not count those generations or identify individual ancient supernovae. In NASA’s May 2024 discovery account, Stefano Carniani and Kevin Hainline described almost ten hours of observations with Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph. The spectrum placed the galaxy at a redshift near 14, within the first few hundred million years of cosmic history. Webb’s Mid-Infrared Instrument supplied another clue. The galaxy was brighter at longer wavelengths than a simple continuation of its shorter-wavelength light would suggest. The team interpreted that excess as evidence for strong emission from ionised gas, including hydrogen and oxygen. That was an inference from brightness measured across a wavelength band. Detecting an individual oxygen line would provide a more specific test. Sander Schouws and colleagues, writing in The Astrophysical Journal, reported a 6.6-sigma detection of the [O III] 88-micrometre line. The notation refers to oxygen atoms that have lost two electrons. Expansion stretched this far-infrared emission into the millimetre wavelengths that ALMA measures. The line gave a redshift of 14.1793, with an uncertainty of 0.0007. That greatly narrowed the earlier Webb estimate while keeping the galaxy firmly within the era before the universe reached 300 million years of age. Carniani’s team, in Astronomy & Astrophysics, obtained a closely matching redshift of 14.1796 from its analysis of the oxygen emission. As ESO’s announcement explains, two teams reached the detection through independent analyses of ALMA data. This agreement strengthens the interpretation of the signal; it is not evidence from two different galaxies. This is ionised oxygen in galactic gas, not a detection of a breathable atmosphere. The early universe began with matter dominated by hydrogen and helium. Substantial oxygen enrichment requires later nuclear processing in stars. ESO describes the sequence behind the finding: stars produce heavier elements, then spread them through their surroundings when they die. The relevant clock is very different from the Sun’s. NASA’s guide to stellar types explains that stellar lifetimes vary enormously with mass. Massive stars consume their fuel quickly and can complete their lives on timescales of millions of years. Their evolving interiors produce heavier nuclei, and supernova explosions can eject enriched material into space. A galaxy therefore does not need billions of years to acquire oxygen. It needs stars to form early enough, some of them to evolve rapidly, and their products to reach the gas being observed. The abundance and distribution of that material depend on how much is produced, mixed, retained or expelled. In our earlier discussion of why Webb’s apparently mature galaxies do not automatically imply impossible ages, the distinction was between chemical development and elapsed time. Oxygen provides evidence of processing. It is not a stopwatch with a fixed number of stellar generations marked on it. Schouws’s team combined the ALMA measurement with Webb information and gas-emission models to estimate a heavy-element abundance roughly five to twenty per cent of the Sun’s. Carniani’s modelling favoured about seventeen per cent of the solar value. These are estimates of chemical abundance relative to a reference composition, not claims that seventeen per cent of the galaxy’s mass is oxygen. The oxygen detection is firmer than every detail of the reconstructed history. Carniani and colleagues also considered whether earlier outflows had removed gas. Such an interpretation depends on estimates of stellar mass, gas content and star-formation history. The authors’ proposed history should remain distinct from the directly measured emission line. NASA dates the formation of our Solar System to about 4.6 billion years ago. The cloud that formed it already included elements made in previous stars. JADES-GS-z14-0 shows that this broader process of stellar manufacture and enrichment was operating far earlier, near the beginning of galaxy formation. The comparison is chronological. It does not establish that oxygen detected in this remote galaxy became part of the Sun or Earth. Our coverage of Webb’s challenge to early galaxy-formation models described the wider problem: bright, active systems appear early, and explaining them requires careful treatment of star formation, gas, dust and feedback. A measured chemical signature adds another constraint to that work. For JADES-GS-z14-0, Carniani’s team identified deeper Webb spectroscopy as a route to a better carbon-to-oxygen measurement. Comparing those elements would help test which stellar populations enriched the gas and how quickly that enrichment occurred. This article is for general information and reflection. title: Korean builders race to invest in Robocon to automate rebar work - CHOSUNBIZ - biz.chosun.com
content: Major builders pour funds into Robocon as labor shortages spur a push for automated rebar handling GS Engineering & Construction and Hoban Construction also invested in Robocon, a robot-based construction automation corporations. Construction companies suffering from labor shortages and rising building costs are moving to secure related technology to replace repetitive and hazardous tasks such as rebar processing with robots. On the 7th, according to the construction industry, the PlanH-XPLOR Green Smart City Venture Investment Partnership, funded by GS Engineering & Construction and Hoban Construction, acquired Robocon's convertible bonds (CB). A CB is a bond that can be converted into the issuing company's stock if certain conditions are met. The fund was jointly formed in 2024 by XPLOR Investment, the corporate venture capital (CVC) of GS Engineering & Construction, and PlanH Ventures, the Hoban Construction CVC. With a total size of 38.5 billion won, the National Land and Transport sector parent fund contributed 15 billion won, GS Engineering & Construction 11.5 billion won, Hoban Construction 2 billion won, and XPLOR Investment 500 million won, among others. A XPLOR Investment official said, "We decided from a strategic investment perspective that can boost productivity at construction sites and accelerate digital transformation, and considering investment revenue," adding, "Several institutions are showing interest in the pre-IPO stage of equity investment before listing, but no additional investment has been decided." Robocon was established in Nov. 2020 when the robotics business unit of Daehan Networks, an affiliate of the DaehanSteel group, was spun off. It develops automation solutions specialized for rebar processing, assembly, and transport. Its flagship solution, "ARON," automates processing steps such as rebar supply, cutting, and bending. According to Robocon, when producing 3,000 tons of rebar for building frames at a rebar processing plant, up to 30 people were previously needed, but introducing ARON can reduce the workforce to fewer than 10. The company said it can cut labor assigned to repetitive tasks and lower material loss that occurs during rebar processing. Robocon's automation solutions have also been adopted at overseas sites, including Singapore's Tuas Port and a project related to Taipei Airport in Taiwan, both built by Korean construction companies. Construction companies are investing in Robocon one after another to address labor shortages at sites and rising construction costs. Automating repetitive tasks that handle heavy materials, such as rebar transport and processing, can raise productivity while also reducing the workforce assigned to hazardous work. Earlier, Samsung C&T invested about 15 billion won in Robocon in 2023 through a fund managed by Samsung Venture Investment. It then secured a majority of board voting rights and, in the second half of the same year, included Robocon as a consolidation subsidiary. Following Samsung C&T, with GS Engineering & Construction and Hoban Construction joining the investment, competition among major builders to secure construction automation technology is entering full swing.

title: GS Caltex and SOOP Supers Trade Key Players to Address Needs - 조선일보
content: Setter Park Sa-rang joins GS Caltex, libero Yu Ga-ram moves to SOOP Supers in strategic roster adjustments [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "I feel sorry and frustrated. But it was a necessary trade for the team…" The voice of Lee Young-taek, GS Caltex head coach, was filled with regret over the phone. Sending away a 21-year-old outside hitter he had nurtured with care since his arrival couldn’t have been easy. GS Caltex and SOOP Supers recently made a surprising trade. SOOP sent setter Park Sa-rang (23), selected first overall in the rookie draft when Pepper Savings Bank was founded, to GS Caltex, while GS Caltex sent libero Yu Ga-ram (21), whom they had been developing intensively, to SOOP. The trade aligned with GS Caltex’s concerns about filling the setter vacancy left by An Hye-jin (free agent) and SOOP’s need to reinforce their libero position, where only Han Da-hye remained as the starting player. Notably, this trade was finalized three days after GS Caltex’s media day. As the defending champion, having achieved an underdog victory last season led by Geisel Silva, the team’s setter issue was a hot topic at the event. Lee Young-taek explained, "We have starting setter Kim Ji-won, and we’ve worked hard to develop backup setters Lee Yoon-shin and Choi Yoon-young. We hired setter specialist coach Ishii Sugu-ru and had them train every night during the offseason. Since setters need experience, we focused on giving these two players more practice matches to build their skills." He added, "Their growth isn’t yet satisfactory, but we’ll keep developing them." However, just three days later, GS Caltex completed the trade to acquire setter Park Sa-rang. A GS Caltex official explained, "We’d been concerned about An Hye-jin’s vacancy, and SOOP reached out with a proposal. The trade filled both teams’ needs. Park Sa-rang is a solid backup for Kim Ji-won." Regarding Yu Ga-ram, the official sighed repeatedly, saying, "She was a player we’d developed so well…" Over the past two seasons, Yu played 64 matches and 213 sets as a defensive reinforcement outside hitter, backup libero, and serve-receive specialist. Last season, her reception efficiency was 36.3% (58/146), effectively supporting Han Su-jin (36.71%, 187/444). She was also seen as a rising franchise star alongside Yu Seo-yeon, Han Su-jin, and Oh Se-yeon. However, with starting libero Han Su-jin firmly established and 19-year-old Kim Hyo-im rapidly growing—even earning a spot on the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games team—the libero position became more stable. Among the three liberos, SOOP specifically targeted Yu Ga-ram. Through this trade, GS Caltex filled their setter vacancy with a proven player. In volleyball, the saying "the game is in the setter’s hands" underscores the difficulty of finding a setter as reliable as Park Sa-rang. Additionally, Kim Ji-won will become a free agent after this season, and An Hye-jin’s return remains uncertain. Even if she returns, her status as a free agent means GS Caltex cannot guarantee her return. Negotiating with two free-agent setters simultaneously would have been complicated, but acquiring Park Sa-rang resolved this. Lee Young-taek sighed, saying, "Yu Ga-ram was hard to let go." However, he added, "Kim Hyo-im grew faster than expected. She seized her opportunity and developed enough to join the Asian Games team. Kim Ji-won alone can’t handle a full season, and our other setters still need time. There were valid reasons for this trade." For SOOP, Park Sa-rang holds special significance as their first overall pick when Pepper Savings Bank was founded. Before the team’s acquisition, SOOP lost outside hitters Park Jeong-ah and Lee Han-bi, creating a vacancy. To address this, they traded their second-round rookie draft pick with Hyundai Engineering & Construction for Seo Ji-hye, and swapped Jung Sol-min with Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK) for Go Ui-jeong and another second-round pick. They also signed Jeon Sae-ah, released by Korea Expressway Corporation, adding depth to their outside hitter position. With Yu Ga-ram’s arrival, they reinforced their libero lineup beyond Han Da-hye and decided to operate with setters Lee Won-jeong and Park Su-bin. A SOOP official explained, "Han Da-hye is excellent, but injuries are a risk. Coach Kim Se-jin was concerned, and the trade with GS Caltex aligned perfectly. We believe Park Su-bin has higher growth potential." SOOP is also anticipating the rookie draft, which now allows overseas Korean players to participate. The new arrangement will supplement the existing role of local police, LCBs and SOGs in detecting NDPS cases. An out-of-turn promotion policy is also in place for personnel who perform high-risk duties during anti-narcotics operations. The police have developed AI-based ‘NARIT’ software to detect dark-web activities, financial trails and international links to drug networks. Scientific investigation is being undertaken to strengthen cases and improve conviction rates. title: Modular AI Data Centers Cut Construction Time to Six Months - Businesskorea
content: A prefabricated modular model that can dramatically reduce the construction time for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers is emerging as a new alternative in the industry. The approach aims to shorten construction timelines from the typical two years to six months or less, allowing infrastructure to begin operating before the performance of the latest graphics processing units (GPUs) deteriorates. LG Uplus said on Sept. 6 that it signed an agreement with GS E&C, Xi C&A, Gansam Architects & Partners and D&O CM to develop a standard model for prefabricated modular data centers (PMDCs). The agreement is significant in that companies with expertise spanning the entire data center lifecycle, from design and construction to operations, have joined forces with the goal of applying the model to actual projects. PMDCs are built by standardizing building structures and power and cooling systems, prefabricating them at a factory and then transporting them to a site for assembly. Since April, the participating companies have been developing a “new-build model” centered on a 100-megawatt (MW) hyperscale PMDC and a “retrofit model” that converts existing buildings into AI data centers. The biggest advantage of the model is its significantly shorter construction time. While conventional building-type data centers take about two years to complete, PMDCs can be completed in six months. As GPU replacement cycles accelerate, construction delays can lead directly to a decline in the value of computing infrastructure, making rapid deployment a key factor directly linked to investment efficiency. The model also offers advantages in quality control and scalability. Because major facilities are manufactured at factories and undergo testing in advance, it can minimize quality variations and the risk of rework that can occur during on-site construction. It also allows modules to be added incrementally as AI demand grows, enabling more flexible operations by expanding capacity as needed. The companies will divide responsibilities based on their respective areas of expertise to improve the model. LG Uplus will define technical requirements and validate the model based on its 27 years of data center operating experience, while GS E&C will handle constructability reviews and process optimization. Xi C&A will focus on power and cooling optimization, while Gansam Architects & Partners and D&O CM will oversee standard design and project management, respectively. Other South Korean companies are also moving to adopt modular construction methods. In March, LG CNS unveiled “AI Box,” a small-scale 1.2 MW data center equipped with 576 GPUs. SK Telecom is also developing a “prefab modular” solution in cooperation with global manufacturers to integrate the production of servers and power infrastructure. Securing power, however, remains a challenge separate from the speed of infrastructure construction. Because AI data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity, faster module production alone cannot accelerate the actual start of operations if grid connections are delayed. An industry official suggested that, given the trend of longer waiting periods for grid access, complementary measures combining energy storage systems (ESS) with intelligent energy management systems should be pursued in parallel. title: GS Engineering & Construction turns to modular tech to speed up AI data center builds - 헤럴드경제
content: Five companies, including GS Engineering & Construction and LG Uplus, sign MOU Partners to jointly develop hyperscale prefabricated modular data center standard model GS Engineering & Construction announced Monday it will develop a standard model for prefabricated modular data centers, or PMDCs, incorporating modular construction technology to meet surging demand for AI data centers. The company signed a "PMDC Alliance" memorandum of understanding Friday at LG Uplus' Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province. GS Engineering & Construction CEO Heo Yun-hong, LG Uplus CEO Hong Beom-sik, Xi C&A CEO Kim Uk-su, Gansam Architects & Partners CEO Park Mu-chan and D&O CM CEO Lee Yeong-ho attended the signing ceremony. In the AI data center market, the rapid spread of generative AI services and growing demand for GPU-based high-performance computing have made "time to market," or TTM — the ability to deliver infrastructure precisely when customers need it — a key competitive differentiator. The PMDC standard model to be developed under the agreement uses a modular approach in which structural components and major systems such as power and cooling are prefabricated off-site and then assembled on location, optimizing the process for faster construction. Through the partnership, each participating company will draw on its own area of expertise to jointly develop and commercialize a hyperscale PMDC standard model applicable to large-scale AI data centers. GS Engineering & Construction will review the PMDC model's architectural structure, construction methods, schedule-reduction strategies and cost appropriateness. Through the collaboration, the company plans to sharpen its PMDC execution capabilities by applying standardization, modularization and schedule-compression measures from the design stage onward — enabling faster and more flexible responses to customer requirements in future AI data center projects and reinforcing its competitiveness in large-scale data center engineering, procurement and construction. "In the AI data center market, the ability to build a data center reliably and quickly — exactly when customers need it — is becoming a critical competitive edge," a GS Engineering & Construction official said. "Through this PMDC collaboration framework, we will continue to strengthen our competitiveness in building AI data centers optimized for the domestic environment." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction recently reported preliminary second-quarter revenue of 2.78 trillion won ($2.04 billion) and operating profit of 91.4 billion won.

title: GS Engineering Launches 48-Story Premium Officetel Near Omokgyo Station - 조선일보
content: Mokdong Yunseul Jai offers schools, hospitals, and 100% lottery system for 651 units GS Engineering & Construction has opened a model house for ‘Mokdong Yunseul Jai’ in Mokdong, Yangcheon-gu, Seoul, and will begin accepting subscription applications on the 8th. Mokdong Yunseul Jai is being developed on the former KT site at 924, 924-3, and 5 Mokdong, Yangcheon-gu, spanning three buildings with six underground floors to 48 above-ground floors, and 651 units with exclusive areas ranging from 114 to 203㎡. Unlike typical small-scale officetels, it focuses on medium-to-large-sized units tailored to premium residential demand, attracting attention as a high-end housing product. Its key advantage is a 100% lottery system, allowing anyone aged 19 or older to apply regardless of subscription account ownership, homeownership status, or residence. ◇Proximity to Omokgyo Station, Mokdong School District Mokdong Yunseul Jai offers excellent accessibility to major business districts like Yeouido and Gangnam via the nearby Omokgyo Station on Seoul Subway Line 5. The complex shares the Mokdong school district, with nearby schools including Seojeong Elementary, Mokun Middle, Yangjeong High, and Jinmyeong Girls’ High, and walking distance to entrance exam academies. Shopping and cultural facilities such as Hyundai Department Store, E-Mart, Megabox, and large medical institutions like Ewha Mokdong Hospital are also nearby. The complex is adjacent to green spaces like Omok Park, Anyangcheon Stream, and Mokdong Comprehensive Sports Center. Unit allocations by exclusive area are as follows: 115㎡A (118 units), 114㎡B (208 units), 114㎡C (118 units), 119㎡A (T1) (45 units), 120㎡A (T2) (30 units), 120㎡A (T3) (15 units), 117㎡C (T1) (45 units), 118㎡C (T2) (45 units), 203㎡AD (10 units), 202㎡BD (9 units), and 198㎡CD (8 units). The complex prioritizes medium-to-large units to cater to demand for spacious living areas. The lower exterior features artist Ned Kahn’s installation ‘Yunseul,’ creating a shimmering facade that reflects sunlight and wind. The basement floors (1–3) will house the ‘Concord Club by Joseon,’ a 9,000㎡ membership wellness club operated by Josun Hotels & Resorts, featuring an indoor pool, fitness center, golf practice range, sauna, and membership lounge. On the 47th floor of Building 102, the ‘Club Cloud’ sky community includes a wine reserve (storage and tasting space), cafeteria, party-style guesthouse, and work/meeting areas. ◇Balcony Design for All Units, Deferred Interest Payment System Units feature 4-bay layouts (living room and three bedrooms aligned in the same direction), two- or three-sided balconies for openness, and some are designed as duplexes. Key appliances such as system air conditioners, air purifiers, refrigerators, washer-dryers, dishwashers, induction cooktops, and microwave ovens, along with kitchen furniture and Italian porcelain tiles and ceramic panels, are provided as standard. Fitness facilities will be directly owned and operated by the developer to reduce fixed management fees for residents. A deferred interest payment system applies, and if the loan interest rate exceeds 2.5% annually, the excess interest will be covered by the project operator. A source from GS Engineering & Construction stated, “Mokdong Yunseul Jai combines a prime location near Omokgyo Station with Mokdong’s educational and lifestyle infrastructure, offering differentiated value. We will strive to establish it as a regional landmark that allows residents to enjoy future value from Mokdong’s redevelopment.” The model house is located at 919-8 Mokdong. Applications will be accepted via the Korea Real Estate Board’s subscription platform from the 8th, with winners announced on the 11th and contracts held on the 13th–14th. Move-in is scheduled for the second half of 2030.

title: The Jamaican Riddim Behind Karol G’s Chart-Topping ‘BbY WOW’ - DancehallMag
content: Karol G’s “BbY WOW” is sitting at number one on Spotify’s Global Top 50, Apple Music’s Global 100, and the Billboard Hot Latin chart, racking up over 78 million streams. But the detail that’s got music heads talking isn’t the chart position, it’s the drum pattern that kicks in around 30 seconds into the song. That pattern belongs to “Coolie Dance Riddim,” a dancehall instrumental built by Jamaican producer Cordel Skatta Burrell back in 2003. Burrell originally created it for a wave of dancehall artists, including Sean Paul, Elephant Man, Bounty Killer, and Ce’Cile, who each put their own style over the beat across two compilation albums released that year. The riddim didn’t stay in dancehall for long. By 2004, it was everywhere, powering Nina Sky and Jabba’s “Move Ya Body” and Pitbull and Lil Jon’s “Culo,” which later got a remix with reggaeton veteran Ivy Queen. If you were near a radio or a dancefloor that year, you heard it constantly. The beat kept moving through the decade. Lumidee and Fatman Scoop flipped it in 2006 for “Dance!,” which also pulled in Whitney Houston’s vocals from “I Wanna Dance With Somebody.” Latin artists like Angel y Khriz rode it on their massive hit “Na De Na,” and Jr Ranks added his own take with “Dale Candela.” The riddim had a way of fitting whatever energy an artist brought to it. After going relatively quiet post-2009, “Coolie Dance Riddim” has had a serious revival over the last six years, and this time it’s artists far outside the Caribbean leading the charge. Argentine artist Ms Nina slowed it down for her 2019 album intro, Spanish rapper Cruzzi gave it a lo-fi texture in 2023, and Kehlani used it as the foundation for “After Hours,” the lead single from her 2024 album CRASH. The riddim has also taken off in Turkey in a big way. Sefo and Demet Akalın’s “Yerinde Dur” has cleared 329 million YouTube views, and Lvbel C5’s “DOGUSSTAN BERI HAKLIYIM” has over 140 million Spotify streams. French DJs HUGEL and SOLTO pulled it into their 2025 house track “Jamaican (Bam Bam)” alongside Sister Nancy’s classic song of the same name. The Arab pop scene has picked it up four times in under a year alone. Moroccan artist DYSTINCT used it on “YAMA,” which has over 212 million YouTube views and 73 million Spotify streams. Egyptian legend Amr Diab, Palestinian Jordanian singer Dana Salah, and Palestinian Chilean artist Elyanna have all followed with their own versions. DYSTINCT says he first heard the riddim as a kid in Belgium on “Move Ya Body” and always knew he wanted to use it. “ The riddim is usable in so many different styles,” he said. “Even if you heard the riddim sampled in so many songs, it still sounds cool and fresh every time.” Dana Salah, who worked with producers Michael Brun and Rami Afuni on her version “Wedding Riddim,” says she heard echoes of Arab dabke music the first time she listened to the beat. “It has such a strong identity: joyful, playful, and sensual, but it also leaves enough space for every artist to find their own melody and culture inside it,” she explained. “More than 20 years later, your body still understands that rhythm before your brain does.” Latin music historian Katelina “La Gata” Eccleston ties the resurgence directly to nostalgia, especially for millennials who were around when the riddim first blew up. “Riddim culture thrives in artists displaying individuality and creativity over a common beat,” she said, “so if an artist is able to invoke a sense of nostalgia by showing homage to another song with a bar or adding to the beat with lyrics that complement its soundscape, then I think the task is completed.” Burrell himself says the global reach of his creation is something he never takes for granted. “From its birth, I’ve always felt its commercial viability,” he said. “ However, witnessing its growth on an international scale is an experience I relish every time there’s another global release.” He’s been publicly supporting artists who sample the riddim on his Instagram, and called “BbY WOW” a “child of the 2000s,” saying Karol G “did a great job.” Burrell also spoke to how his Jamaican roots shape everything he makes, even when he’s aiming for something with wider reach. “I’ve always tried not to get stuck in a dancehall-only approach, instead drawing inspiration from global music that I’ve connected with,” he said. “The next step was making it palatable for the world to appreciate.” With Karol G’s version now sitting at the top of global charts and new artists in Turkey, France, and across the Arab world still finding fresh ways into the beat, the list of songs built on “Coolie Dance Riddim” keeps growing. title: Watchdog editor's favorite happy hour spot is unassuming from outside - Treasure Coast News
content: It's not the place many people think of as their favorite water hole. It doesn't fit the Treasure Coast stereotype of a tiki hut by the beach. But TCPalm Watchdog Editor Arnie Rosenberg was introduced to Kyle G's Oyster and Wine Bar when he moved to Port St. Lucie three years ago, and it became an instant favorite. Part of the Kyle G Restaurants group, the Oyster Bar is not only a fine-dining restaurant, but it's also the spot for delicious appetizers, innovative drinks and a great vibe. The bartenders bring their own dose of fun to happy hour. Take your choice from among specialty drinks ranging from vodka offerings to concoctions of bourbon, gin, vodka, tequila and cognac. My choice almost always is the Blue Barracuda 2.0, made with coconut rum, pineapple, creme de banana, lime and blue curacao. And it's served on fire. Yeah, really, with flames enveloping the glass. Snack to your heart's content from Kyle G's happy hour menu. Want to stay with the restaurant's seafood theme? Go for the lobster and shrimp dip or tuna tataki. Have a taste for something more filling? Dig into some Korean BBQ ribs, curry spiced lamb sliders or bourbon steak sliders. Want to try eating a little healthy? There's always the mini California roll stacks or mussels from Prince Edward Island. There's a wide choice of raw bar items, fresh fish, seafood and chicken, all served with innovative sauces and sides in hand crafted presentations. It's at 1724 St. Lucie West Blvd. in Port St. Lucie.

title: LG Uplus Launches Alliance to Speed Up AI Data Center Construction - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Partnership Signed With GS E&C and Xi C&A
Group to Develop Standard PMDC Model LG Uplus is jointly developing a standard model for prefabricated modular data centers (PMDC) with GS E&C and Xi C&A to meet surging demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. LG Uplus (032640.KS) said on the 6th that it signed a memorandum of understanding to build a PMDC alliance with GS E&C (006360.KS), Xi C&A, Gansam Architects & Partners and D&O CM on the 4th at its Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province. Under the PMDC approach, building structures along with power and cooling equipment are standardized and prefabricated at a factory before being assembled on site. Compared with conventional site-based construction, the method shortens build times and improves quality consistency. Drawing on expertise in design, construction, operations and project management, the alliance members have been jointly working since April to develop a standard model that can be applied to actual AI data center (AIDC) projects. Through the agreement, the partners plan to complete a PMDC model competitive not only in South Korea but globally, and to apply it to actual AIDC construction projects. LG Uplus will define operating standards and technical requirements for PMDC, set business direction and validate the model, based on experience accumulated from building and operating data centers nationwide as well as its AIDC in Paju. GS E&C will provide constructability reviews, process optimization and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) capabilities for newly built PMDC models, drawing on its experience in large-scale data center construction and field execution. Xi C&A will handle the development of a retrofit model that can be applied to existing buildings, along with power and cooling optimization. "We will create a PMDC model with global-level competitiveness and continue strengthening our competitiveness in building next-generation AIDCs," said Hong Beom-shik, chief executive of LG Uplus. title: Fans share their feelings ahead of Karol G’s Sun Bowl Performance - KVIA
content:
EL PASO, Texas (KVIA) - Karol G begins her weekend of performances at the Sun Bowl Saturday as part of her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour and fans told ABC-7 why she is one of their favorite artists. The fans came from across the country beginning with Texas's neighboring state New Mexico as fans from Deming, Roswell, and the town of Arrey told ABC-7 they made the trip to come see the Colombian singer. Angelica Castañeda, a fan from Roswell, said she drove her daughters 3 hours so they could see Karol G since they are all fans and for Angelica it helps relieve her stress. "For me, when I hear it, it just kind releases my stress and I just play her music and I feel better," Castañeda said. Another fan from New Mexico, Jaileen Loera from Arrey, said it helps her feel 'heard' through the artist's music. "I feel heard, she does a big confidence boost in latinas, we are overseen I want to say when it comes to showing our feelings," Loera said. "I feel like she made it very big to like, speak about your feelings and it's okay to feel a lot and not be over exaggerating about it you know." Lala Castle, a fan who made the trip to El Paso from Chicago, mentioned something similar when mentioning the emotional response the music brings out of her and specifically mentioning when the music brings up love and men. "She talks about love, she talks about how men actually are, some," Castle said. "She puts you in your feelings, she puts you in your thoughts as well and she also talks good about them to. So it's a little bit of everything." Castle said she has seen the musician perform in Chicago, saying the 'vibe' of the show Karol G puts on is something like a 'new kind of excitement' that will not disappoint. "It's freaking amazing," Castle said. "The vibe is like, boom, very exciting. It's like a little taste of excitement that you'll never experience." Karol G is the latest major artist to come to El Paso after Coldplay in June of 2025 and BTS in May of this year with Chris Brown and Usher scheduled to perform in the Sun Bowl next in October. After coming to see the city herself, Castle gave her opinion as to why more artist are choosing to add El Paso to their tour. "I mean, look at the people. They're so friendly, they're so welcoming. Coming from Chicago, a big city coming to El Paso, like, they're so united," Castle said. Karol G's performance on Saturday will begin at 7 p.m. with doors opening at 5 p.m. and Sunday's performance also begins at 7 p.m. KVIA ABC 7 is committed to providing a forum for civil and constructive conversation. title: FTU pushes for immediate restoration of teachers’ salaries - Fiji Sun
content: Where necessary, he said the union would consider further action to protect the rights and welfare of affected members. Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) general secretary Muniappa Goundar in Suva on June 6, 2026. With the third school term beginning tomorrow, the Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) says its immediate priority is ensuring every legitimate teacher affected by the Pay 18 salary stoppage is verified and has their pay restored as quickly as possible. FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said the union had engaged with the Ministry of Education to identify individual cases, help members address any outstanding documentation and ensure teachers who were genuinely employed and performing their duties were not left without income. Where necessary, he said the union would consider further action to protect the rights and welfare of affected members. “The FTU accepts that teachers have a responsibility to sign and return appointment documents within the required timeframe,” Mr Goundar said. “However, we do not accept that the matter can simply be attributed to teachers alone.” Mr Goundar said the Ministry had previously acknowledged administrative, human resource and processing problems, including documents being submitted to the wrong officers and delays within the system. He said the recent payroll verification demonstrated weaknesses on both sides and responsibility should be examined fairly rather than placing the entire burden on teachers. “At this stage, the ministry has not provided the FTU with a definitive blanket timeline for restoration of salaries to all 134 teachers,” he said. “Our position is that once an affected teacher’s employment, appointment and documentation have been verified, payment should be restored without unnecessary delay, including payment of all salary arrears properly due.” The FTU supports the Ministry’s responsibility to verify its payroll and prevent public funds from being improperly paid. However, Mr Goundar said if an employee whose contract had expired was able to remain on the payroll and receive salary payments until Pay 18/2026, questions needed to be asked about the effectiveness of the Ministry’s human resource, payroll and verification controls. “The fact that the verification followed recommendations in the Auditor-General’s 2024 report makes it even more important that the ministry explain what controls were previously in place and why these discrepancies were not detected earlier,” he said. An email seeking clarification has been sent to Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary Navin Raj. It remained unanswered when this edition went to press yesterday.

title: LG Uplus Unveils Modular AI Data Center Model to Cut Construction Time - 조선일보
content: Collaborating with GS Engineering & Construction and others, LG Uplus standardizes AI infrastructure with prefabricated modular tech, reducing project timelines LG Uplus is collaborating with industry partners to jointly develop a standardized prefabricated modular data center (PMDC) model incorporating modular technology. The strategy aims to establish a cooperative framework to shorten construction periods and standardize quality for AI data centers (AIDC) in response to the rapidly growing demand for AI infrastructure. LG Uplus announced on September 6 that it signed a business agreement on September 4 with GS Engineering & Construction, Jai C&A, Gansam Architecture, and D&O CM at the Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province, to form a PMDC alliance. The PMDC under development standardizes building structures, power, and cooling facilities, which are prefabricated in factories and assembled on-site using a modular approach. Compared to traditional on-site construction, this method reduces project timelines, ensures quality standardization, and allows flexible infrastructure supply in response to changing demand. With the recent AI boom driving surging demand for data centers, the ability to rapidly supply AI infrastructure has become a key competitive factor in the industry. Consequently, PMDC, which offers supply flexibility and operational efficiency, is gaining attention as a next-generation data center model. The alliance members have jointly pursued standard model development since April, leveraging their respective expertise to apply PMDC to actual AI data center projects. They reviewed a hyperscale PMDC model for large-scale AI data centers consuming 100MW-class power and a retrofit model for converting existing buildings into data centers. Subsequently, they finalized detailed designs and technical specifications tailored to South Korea’s data center environment, along with each company’s roles and business execution framework. LG Uplus will establish operational standards and technical requirements for PMDC based on its experience in constructing and operating nationwide data centers and the Paju AIDC. It will also lead business direction setting and model verification. GS Engineering & Construction will review architectural structures, construction methods, timeline reduction strategies, and cost appropriateness for PMDC models applied to new sites, drawing on its experience in large-scale data center projects. LG Uplus CEO Hong Bum-shik stated, “In the AI era, the core competitive edge for data centers lies in the ability to build necessary infrastructure promptly in line with rapidly changing customer demands. We will strengthen our competitiveness in next-generation AIDC construction by developing a globally competitive PMDC model.”

title: LG U+ has joined hands with domestic construction and design companies such as GS Engineering - mk.co.kr
content:
LG U+ has joined hands with domestic construction and design companies such as GS Engineering & Construction and Jai C&A to develop a pre-production modular data center (PMDC) standard model. As demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure surges, the ability to build data centers faster emerges as competitive, this is to secure a cooperative system that can reduce the construction period. LG U+ announced on the 6th that it signed a "business agreement to build a PMDC alliance" with GS Engineering & Construction, Jai C&A, Gansam Architecture, and D&OCM at Pyeongchon Mega Center in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province on the 4th. The signing ceremony was attended by executives of each company, including LG Uplus CEO Hong Bum-sik, GS Engineering & Construction CEO Huh Yoon-hong, Zai C&A CEO Kim Wook-soo, Gansam Architecture CEO Park Moo-chan, and D&OMC CEO Lee Young-ho. PMDC is a data center that assembles building structures, power and cooling facilities in advance at the factory with standard standards and then on-site. Compared to the conventional method of constructing most of the facilities on site, the construction period is shorter, it is easier to keep the quality constant, and the scale can be flexibly increased as demand changes. As demand for data centers surged due to the spread of AI, the ability to supply infrastructure on time has emerged as the core of industry competitiveness, and PMDC, which can quickly build, expand, and operate at the same time, is drawing attention as a next-generation construction model. Since April, alliance participants have jointly developed a standard model to apply PMDC to actual AI data center (AIDC) projects. Based on the 100MW hyperscale PMDC, the new built-in model on the site and retrofit (retrofit) model that converts existing buildings to AI infrastructure were reviewed together to specify designs and technology specifications optimized for the domestic environment. The roles were divided. LG U+ is in charge of defining operating standards and technical requirements, establishing business directions, and verifying models based on its experience in establishing and operating data centers and Paju AIDC nationwide. In particular, it plans to reflect 99.999% of uninterrupted operation know-how that has been maintained for 27 years from the design stage. GS Engineering & Construction is in charge of reviewing the constructability of new built-in models, optimizing processes, and designing, procuring, and constructing (EPC) based on its experience in large-scale data center construction. Jai C&A is in charge of developing retrofit models and optimizing power and cooling using its experience in building mechanical, electric, and piping (MEP), while Gansam Architecture is in charge of data center-specific design. D&OCM provides project management and construction project management (CM) capabilities. The company explains that it is a regular cooperation system that goes beyond a one-off collaboration in that companies covering the entire data center cycle from design to construction, operation, and business management have come together. In addition, LG U+ plans to increase the completeness of the PMDC model by combining the AIDC construction capabilities within LG Group and the design and construction capabilities of external specialized companies, and use it to build AIDC in the future to strengthen the group-level business competitiveness. "The AI-era data center's core competitiveness is the ability to build necessary infrastructure in a timely manner to meet customer demand," said Hong Bum-sik, CEO of LG Uplus. "As professional companies have gathered their capabilities to apply actual businesses, we will continue to strengthen our competitiveness to build next-generation AIDC by creating global-level PMDC models." ※ This article was translated using AI technology for reader convenience. title: The Short Lived Performance Car That Deserved Better - HotCars
content: Jared has spent 15 years covering the auto industry, getting his first break with autoX—one of Asia’s biggest auto magazines. Since 2010, he has reviewed hundreds of cars and motorbikes around the world, worked with Top Gear, Autocar, Evo, Motoring World, and Quattroruote, served on the IMOTY jury for five years, and is a founding member of the Automotive Journalist Association of India (AJAI). Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update BMW M-Cars wrote the rulebook for the performance sedan. Audi has long been a formidable presence in the segment, and Mercedes perfected the "German muscle car" with their V8-powered AMGs, but credible non-German challengers have always been rare. What makes the landscape even more challenging is that the market has been shifting decisively away from traditional performance vehicles. Sports cars are few and far between, coupes that are not dedicated sports cars are nearly extinct, and SUVs and crossovers have become the default choice for most buyers. The SUV craze began in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with pioneers like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V anchoring the economy end of the spectrum, while the Mercedes-Benz ML and the Lexus RX300 effectively invented the modern luxury crossover class. With crossovers now the industry standard, performance cars have had to evolve in tandem. You can't build a performance variant of a vehicle you no longer sell — and since automakers are moving crossovers the way McDonald's moves burgers and fries, while sedans are quietly fading like Circuit City and RadioShack, it only makes sense that the ranks of performance sedans and coupes have thinned considerably. There is nothing inherently wrong with something like the X5M, but performance sedans have always held a special appeal for enthusiasts that no SUV has quite managed to replicate. Thankfully, there are still some fantastic performance sedans on the market — but there is one in particular that deserved to stick around a little longer. The muscle car is American, the exotic sports car Italian, and the performance saloon German. Obviously, this is a generalization, but such widely held perceptions of certain market segments have a real impact on how consumers shop. A common critique levied at something like the Genesis G90 is that it isn't quite up to the standard of the S-Class. That isn't entirely untrue, but buyers often begin their evaluation of a Genesis, Acura, Cadillac, or Lexus by assuming it could never surpass a “proper” German luxury sedan. While American, Japanese, and Korean automakers have all built exceptional luxury and performance sedans, overcoming those deeply ingrained perceptions remains an uphill battle. Much like General Motors and John DeLorean inventing the muscle car in 1964, BMW ostensibly invented the modern sports sedan in 1984 with the introduction of the E28 M5. The first-ever M5 was powered by a 3.5L I6 that produced 256 horsepower in the North American market. The iconic E30 M3 arrived just two years later, and two years after that the second-generation M5, the E34, upped displacement to 3.6L (3.8L post-facelift in Europe) and pushed output past 300 horsepower. And if the E34 didn't cement the M5 legacy, the legendary 4.9L V8-powered E39 most certainly did. Mercedes followed suit in 1993 with the first production AMG, the C36. In the years that followed, some incredible cars continued the lineage — the C36 gave way to the V8-powered C43, C55, and C63. The E39 was succeeded by the 5.0L V10-powered E60, and Audi was busy fitting V8s and V10s into its S and RS cars throughout the 2000s. Just as the Mustang defined the pony car, these German sports sedans defined their segment, making it that much harder for outside competitors to carve out a lasting place. Find a car enthusiast and ask them which sports sedan on the current market would be their pick. If you ask me? I'll take a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, thank you very much. And it's not just because you get a 6.2L supercharged V8 producing 650 horsepower — borrowed from the C7 Z06 — paired with the brilliant MagneRide suspension. No, despite my great appreciation for many automatics, I simply prefer a manual transmission. I'm certainly not in the minority, and aside from the M3, Cadillac is the only other game in town when it comes to rowing your own gears in a four-door sedan. No manual has been offered in the M5 since the F10 generation, and no manual has appeared in an Audi sports sedan since the B8.5 S4 — or the B7 RS4 if you want the full-fat performance model. Cadillac, meanwhile, offers both the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing with 6-speed manuals. The CT5-V Blackwing is the spiritual heir to the original V-car, the CTS-V. When it arrived in 2004 with the 405-horsepower LS6 V8 borrowed from the C5 Corvette Z06, it was the last thing anyone expected from Cadillac. At the time, the brand was riding high on the second-generation Escalade and still selling the DeVille and Seville. There was already plenty of surprise in 2003 when the CTS 3.6L became the first Cadillac offered with a manual transmission since the 1988 Cimarron — nobody was expecting the original CTS-V on top of that, let alone a second generation that paired a manual transmission with 556 supercharged horsepower from the LSA V8. We're quite lucky the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing models have carried that torch, because the Pontiac GXP and Chevy SS came and went faster than the Honda Prologue. The Cadillac offerings have been among the absolute best in this segment for the better part of two decades. The CTS-V and ATS-V — and their successors, the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing — are arguably even better than their respective M5 and M3 counterparts, proving that American brands have a legitimate claim in this space. Japanese and Korean brands have made attempts, but have struggled to establish a long-term foothold. Aside from Lexus, Infiniti and Genesis are the only two of the bunch to have offered a V8, but the M56/Q70 5.6L and G80 5.0L fall well short of true sports sedan status. The Kia Stinger GT2, Genesis G70 3.3T, Infiniti Q50 Red Sport, and Acura TLX Type S are all fantastic cars, but they compete more directly with cars like the S4, M340i, C43 AMG, and the CT4-V (non-Blackwing) than with M Division, AMG, or Blackwing at the top. Lexus is really the only one of the bunch to have genuinely gone after BMW — first with the IS-F, and then with one of the all-time great performance sedans. The GS-F was based on the fourth-generation Lexus GS, introduced in 2011. Unlike the previous generation of GS, which offered V8 trims such as the GS 400, 430, and 460, the final iteration of the Lexus GS was V6-only. It was an excellent V6 — the 3.5L 2GR-FE/FKS — but it didn't quite pack the punch of the V8 cars. That's fine, though, because for the final generation Lexus saved the V8 for something more special: the GS-F. While the previous V8 trims were essentially engine upgrades, the GS-F was a proper sports sedan. It was Lexus's second entry into that market, following the 2008–2014 IS-F. It used the same 8-speed automatic and 5.0L V8 as the IS-F, but produced 51 more horsepower than its predecessor. And as noted, the GS-F is far more than just an engine. Starting in 2017, models received adaptive variable suspension (AVS), which allows the car to adjust the dampers independently across 30 different settings based on driver input, selected mode, and real-time sensor data. All GS-F models also received a torque-vectoring differential that can be set to standard, slalom, or track mode. This is not to be confused with brake torque vectoring, as found on a Fiesta ST — this is a proper mechanical trick diff that automotive journalists consistently praised for allowing this large sedan to rotate through corners like a much smaller machine. The GS-F was also fitted with Brembo 6-piston front and 4-piston rear brakes, giving the driver genuine confidence when scrubbing off speed. The GS-F shares the same wonderful powertrain as the IS-F and RC-F, using the same Aisin AA80E 8-speed automatic — though the GS-F has a shorter final drive ratio than the IS-F and RC-F — and the 2UR-GSE 5.0L V8. Which is to say, it works. The AA80E, which debuted in the 2007 LS 460 as the world's first production 8-speed automatic, has earned an excellent long-term reputation. It most recently appeared in the IS 500 F Sport Performance, which shares the same mechanical core as the proper F models. Both the 2UR-GSE and the Aisin 8-speed are genuinely reliable units. In fact, the entire car is, which is why these have held 60%–70% of their value since new. According to classic.com and comparable sales from major auction sites, the GS-F is currently valued at nearly double that of an equivalent M5 from the same era, despite the performance gap. It's true that contemporary rivals — the aforementioned M5, CTS-V, E63, and RS7 — all made more power and could outpace the GS-F's already brisk 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph. That was a legitimate critique when the car was new, but 467 horsepower and 389 lb-ft of torque are not small numbers. We've been desensitized to power figures that include a comma, but a 193-inch, 4,100-pound sedan reaching 60 mph in the same time as a 981 Cayman S is genuinely impressive. And besides — are you really taking this to the track? Are you racing for pinks? The GS-F may not have been the outright performance king of its era, but given its reliability and its glorious engine note, it deserved another chance. It only lasted five model years, after all. Sadly, though it's possible Toyota could one day fit the 4.0L twin-turbo V8 from the GR GT3 into a new Lexus sports sedan, the sedan market may not survive long enough for that to happen. Lexus currently only offers the front-wheel-drive ES in the sedan segment. Thankfully, the GS-F appears reliable enough to last for decades — just don't expect prices to fall; the market has already figured out how special these cars are. It's just a shame there won't be another. Luxury performance sedans are notorious for shedding value once they leave the showroom. The Lexus GS F hasn't escaped depreciation entirely, but it has aged far more gracefully on the used market than its German rivals. With an original MSRP ranging from about $84,440 for 2016 models to more than $90,000 for a well-optioned 2020 example, the GS F has become more attainable over time, yet it remains remarkably resistant to the steep value drops that typically define this segment. Today, early 2016–2017 cars typically trade anywhere from the high-$30,000s to around $50,000, depending on mileage and condition, while facelifted 2018–2020 examples — which received updated styling and additional standard technology — regularly command well over $50,000. Exceptional low-mileage cars can fetch considerably more, as demonstrated by a 20,000-mile 2020 GS F that sold for $73,500 on Bring a Trailer in early 2025. Meanwhile, buyers can still pick up an F10 BMW M5 for less than $30,000, and even the rare S212 Mercedes-Benz E 63 AMG often changes hands for under $40,000. The contrast highlights just how well the GS F has protected its value. Lexus' hard-earned reputation for reliability is undoubtedly part of the equation, but it's far from the only reason. Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability is certainly part of the reason the GS F has depreciated far less than its European rivals, but it's far from the whole story. There are other reasons, starting with sheer rarity. The collector market tends to reward cars that combine genuine performance with genuine scarcity, and the Lexus GS F checks both boxes. While BMW and Mercedes-AMG built their M5 and E63 in far greater numbers, Lexus produced roughly 4,823 GS Fs worldwide during the model's five-year run, with only about 2,347 examples reaching U.S. buyers. Special editions and uncommon specifications only amplify that exclusivity — the 2019 10th Anniversary Edition was capped at 100 U.S. cars, while rare finishes such as Flare Yellow and Molten Pearl have become especially sought-after among enthusiasts. Just as important is what's under the hood. The GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8 belongs to a rapidly shrinking breed of naturally aspirated performance engines, particularly in the sports sedan world. It rewards drivers with immediate throttle response, a broad and predictable power curve, a 7,300-rpm redline, and an exhaust note that no turbocharged engine can quite replicate. Those qualities are even more compelling today, given that there is no naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan currently on sale. After spending so much time praising the GS F, it's fair to ask why Lexus discontinued it after the 2020 model year. The answer has less to do with the GS F itself and more to do with the fate of the GS sedan it was built upon. By the end of its run, the GS had become financially unsustainable. Lexus sold just 3,378 GSs in the U.S. during 2019, accounting for only 4% of the brand's passenger-car sales and less than 1% of the midsize luxury sedan segment. The GS was also squeezed from both sides. Buyers seeking comfort overwhelmingly chose the less expensive ES, while those wanting practicality flocked to the RX, which routinely sold well into six figures annually. With engineering resources increasingly directed toward crossovers, the aging fourth-generation GS received only incremental updates, leaving its interior technology and overall package trailing newer European competitors. As impressive as the GS F was, it couldn't reverse those trends. Against 600-plus-horsepower twin-turbo rivals like the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E 63, its 467-horsepower naturally aspirated V8 appealed to a niche audience. Combined with Lexus' smaller performance-brand footprint, the GS F simply wasn't enough to save the GS nameplate. The GS F belongs to a category that has effectively disappeared. You can no longer walk into a dealership and buy a naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan. Nearly every manufacturer has downsized to turbocharged six-cylinder engines or electrified powertrains in pursuit of stricter emissions targets and improved fuel economy. Even the remaining V8-powered performance sedans rely almost exclusively on forced induction to achieve their staggering power figures. They are undeniably quicker, but they lack the immediate throttle response, progressive power delivery, and intoxicating high-revving character that defined the GS F. To its credit, Lexus kept that philosophy alive a little longer with the IS 500 F SPORT Performance. Sharing the GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8, the smaller sedan produced a slightly improved 472 horsepower and wrapped it in a lighter, more agile package that many enthusiasts considered the spiritual successor to the GS F. The IS 500 F SPORT Performance demonstrated that Lexus still believed there was an audience for a naturally aspirated V8 luxury sports sedan, but it ultimately proved not large enough to overcome market realities.     Production ended after the 2025 model year, bringing Lexus' naturally aspirated V8 sedan lineage to a close. As emission regulations tighten and electrification accelerates, cars like the GS F are becoming relics of a different era. Enthusiasts continue to ask for naturally aspirated V8 sports sedans, but the industry is moving in a different direction. That only makes the GS F more desirable today — not just as a great driver's car, but as a reminder of a performance philosophy that may never return.
